But Peter Caulfield, founder of Save Our Voices Now which campaigns against AI voice cloning, expressed some disquiet about the project, and the fact Motson had been unable to consent to it.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9gk: I've just spent a week using Muse, Meta's AI agent that rolls out in the UK today.
Agents are systems that don't just respond to questions but can carry out tasks for you. With Muse, Meta gives the examples of "searching for a cheaper energy deal" or "sorting the school calendar."
And it's true that it has helped me run my life - but it also challenged my personal privacy boundaries, and made me endure some cringeworthy interactions.
It has made a truly enormous bet on AI - of the $145bn (£111bn) it will spend this year much of it will be on building out the tech.

For that to pay off we all need to start using it much more, and Meta hopes Muse will do for AI agents what WhatsApp did for messaging - that is, become the AI agent of choice for billions of people, putting Meta at the forefront of the AI revolution.
But it's not just about what consumers think. Regulators are keeping a careful eye on these emerging tools too.
"Agentic AI has significant potential to benefit people and businesses", the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) noted as Muse launched in the UK.

But its chief executive, Paul Arnold, added it had been "clear with Meta about its responsibilities under data protection law prior to launch, particularly the requirement to ensure that users and the wider public can meaningfully understand and control how their personal data is used in the Muse product".
Muse bills itself as a personal AI agent available to anyone aged 18 and over.
"It doesn't just answer questions, it actually goes out and does work for you," said David Singleton, Meta's VP of engineering on AI products.
"So it helps people stay on top of things," he added. "[It] helps you take tasks and projects off your plate, and also helps you turn your long-term goals into action plans."

What this means is you can set it up to do something for you, like find some specific holiday options, and it will work away on that even as you move off the app and get on with your day, reporting back once it has finished.
It won't book the holiday without your permission - but it can then make the purchase, if you let it.
And the permission requests keep on coming. Every time Muse wants to do something, send something or post something, you have to allow it.

It is reassuring to know that an AI agent isn't running amok in your name, even if it also gets a bit annoying, though you can give it more autonomy (and so get fewer messages) if you adjust the settings.
Muse can't access many apps at the moment but the fundamental ones are the most personal.
I found myself wincing as I hooked it up to one of my personal email accounts, my personal calendar and my personal phone messages. I did not allow it any access to my BBC accounts.
It can't access WhatsApp except to set up a separate chat between it and the user, and while it found me some train tickets, it could not book them via the app which I use, and which is cheaper.

Amazon has blocked it from its marketplace, citing data security concerns but my agent didn't seem to know that, and spent a fruitless hour repeatedly telling me it was still waiting for the page to load in order to find me some shelves.
A number of big UK firms are working with Meta though, including Marks & Spencer, Debenhams Group, Currys, Sainsbury's and Ocado.
The ICO is urging consumers to be cautious with AI agents though: "consider the pros and cons," it said in a blog post to coincide with Muse's launch. , external
"Agents can make mistakes. Mistakes can be magnified if the agent is acting autonomously," it noted.
Meta is keen to emphasise how its agents can be personalised: "No two Muses are alike," , external it says in its press release.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv98: The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.

The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as a spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.

When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.

Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take .
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq62: A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia
Nvidia's market value rose by nearly $1 trillion as its share price skyrocketed after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect.

His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly.
Nvidia shares rose by more than 31% which also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing by 6.5% and the S&P 500 also rose 4.75%.
Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday , with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced.
Other chipmakers experienced large increases following Monday's announcement from the Nvidia board. Shares in Micron Technology jumped 19%, while AMD shares rose nearly 7%.
Tesla shares also lept up by nearly 11.5%, while other tech gains were more muted by comparison: Amazon shares were up nearly 3.5%, and Apple and Microsoft rose by less than 2%.
While the surge in Nvidia shares was large and drove its market value back towards $4tn, the firm's share price remains about 21% down from a month ago.
A sharp drop occurred on 4 November, after the Democrat's midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come led to a broad tech stock sell-off.

On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its accounting practices.
Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry.

Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said - but US President Donald Trump has claimed he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang.
Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector".
"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said.
"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said Huang's reinstatement was an astonishing about-turn for Nvidia, particularly given reports of an as-yet unconfirmed SEC investigation.

"This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world's most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable," he said.
"Today's stock market rebound represents a massive sigh of relief by investors. However, one cannot rule out a more conservative approach by Huang going forward.
"His every move will be scrutinised by the market, and he may wish to tread more carefully to protect his integrity and ensure that Nvidia is being run responsibly."

Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said Huang's reinstatement "reportedly at the encouragement of Trump Administration officials and without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation."
She added: "What is abundantly clear is that the AI industry requires guardrails and oversight."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c687: Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.
That central position prompted questions, in the aftermath of Huang's departure over revelations of extramarital affairs, over how important he was to the wider AI industry and US economy.
The fact he has been handed his job back after just 11 days in a U-turn by Nvidia's board implies the top brass believe Huang is irreplaceable.
Shares in the company have surged on the news of Huang's shock return, following a period of sharp declines.
While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.
The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.
Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.
It is now one the most valuable firms in the world and its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.
Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on it, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.
Some suggested his departure, which was sparked by the emergence that Huang had an affair with a woman alleged to have been a spy for China, posed a risk to the wider AI industry.

That was because it was unclear whether Nvidia would change strategy and potentially rein in spending - a move could have had wider implications for the US economy, but which looks unlikely now Huang has returned.

The fears were sparked due to Nvidia being a key source of finance for many firms, as well as being a microchip supplier. On its journey to the top of the AI industry, it has, through Huang, created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?
That risk was perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, had called for Huang's reinstatement.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, and backed a campaign, along with shareholders and supporters, to "Bring Jensen Back".
Following the announcement of Huang's return, Musk posted: "The mistake has been corrected."
Kathleen Brooks, research director at investment platform XTB, said Huang's return suggested he was "the godfather" of AI and has the status to shift "the dial for corporate finance".

"Is Jensen Huang the most valuable man on the planet? His return suggests more of the same when it comes to circular financing and the rapid AI infrastructure build out, and the market loves it," she added.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmze: For a long time it seemed that Jensen Huang, the leather jacket-clad founder of Nvidia, dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", could do no wrong.
Then came allegations of two affairs - one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy - that rocked the world of tech and the global stock market. Huang resigned.
Now, just 11 days later, he's been reinstated by the board, who says it believes he is the right person to lead the company.
So what do we know about the man who is once again at the head of Nvidia, a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China?
Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.
The company is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.
Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.

His remarkable rise to the top of his profession saw him amass an estimated fortune of close to $200bn earlier this year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, though that has since dropped to around $105bn.

Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia.

The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after tech giant rocked by second affair allegation

Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on a par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products.

So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit".
But while Huang is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he said.
Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very important to him".

First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman associated with Singapore-based firm Megaspeed is a Chinese intelligence asset.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqpv: During the trial, the prosecution described Kurtaj as a "leading light" in the teen gang Lapsus$
A cyber criminal who hacked the maker of Grand Theft Auto has been released on licence on the same day as being sentenced to 7 years in prison.
Multiple offender Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, was released from custody with the judge warning him: "Don't let this happen again."
The now 21-year-old hacked several companies and individuals, including GTA 6-maker Rockstar Games, whom he tried to extort after stealing clips of the unfinished game in 2022.
Kurtaj had pleaded guilty last Monday at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.
Kurtaj was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.
But, in an unusual move, he was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.
Now, he has been sentenced and released on the same day as the judge considered his hospital stay and remand in prison long enough.
He has been given a Serious Crime Prevention Order which will last five years. It restricts his activity online including barring him from using Telegram and Discord.
City of London Police said the case "highlights the dangers that young people can end up being drawn to online".
He hacked Rockstar games, Revolut and Uber while on bail and under police protection in a Travelodge in Bicester.
He was there for protection from rival hackers who had threatened to attack him for his stolen stashes of Bitcoin.
With his computer confiscated, Kurtaj hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into his hotel room television along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.
He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished GTA 6, which had been shrouded in secrecy until its release last week.
He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."
The company refused to co-operate so he posted the clips and source code on a forum under the username TeaPotUberHacker.
Rockstar Games said it cost the firm $5m (£3.8m) to recover from the hack, plus thousands of hours of staff time.
The company also said the breach revealed for the first time that one of the playable characters in the game was a woman - a secret it was guarding closely for marketing purposes.
He had short hair and an unkempt beard and wore a suit and buttoned-up white shirt without a tie.
The Judge Mr Justice Turner told him "you are a very talented young man," and warned him: "Don't let this happen again."
Kurtaj's defence team said he found the online world a more comfortable way of interacting with other people.

"The restricted and repetitive patterns of behaviour and interests that are a core feature of ASD [autism spectrum disorder] led him to become preoccupied with the online world where he felt better able to function and exist," they said.
They said he was exposed to people who showed him how to cheat at games and then to "people who were involved in hacking".
During the pandemic, he was "very isolated" and his "connection to Lapsus$ provided him with a sense of community and self-worth that had been absent in his life previously," they added.
Kurtaj's Snapchat posts were the first sign for reporters that he had been released from a secure hospital

Kurtaj and the gang's other hacks on BT/EE, Revolut and Uber used social engineering techniques - tricking people into clicking malicious links or giving up sensitive information - to gain access to internal systems.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe9: Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.
Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.
Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.
The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it's now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.

Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up , external in San Francisco.
Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.

But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn , external that this was a possibility.

Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).
Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker employed in the city is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study , external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Leny Yoro will be available for Manchester United's game against Brentford on Saturday after his one-match ban was rescinded
Leny Yoro's overturned red card against Liverpool appears to have turned into an unseemly difference of opinion between Manchester United and referees' body Pro Ref.
Yoro was sent off after bringing down Liverpool striker Alexander Isak in the eighth minute of the 4-0 defeat at Anfield.
Referee Sam Barrott sent off the France international, and the decision was backed up by video assistant referee (VAR) John Brooks.
It split opinion among pundits and fans. Would Isak have got to the ball before goalkeeper Senne Lammens? Was it really a clear goalscoring chance?
First, a Football Association regulatory commission upheld United's appeal and cancelled the red card.
Then Pro Ref boss Howard Webb said the red card was not "clearly wrong" - just moments before United held a pre-match news conference.
Over to Red Devils head coach Mauricio Pochettino, who was fiercely critical of the decision, and in particular the VAR.
But how can Pro Ref still believe the decision was right when an FA commission said it was wrong?
So United won their appeal. Pro Ref would disagree. Could the two sides not just agree to differ?
"You ask me a question and I need to defend our situation and our club and our players," Pochettino said about Yoro's red card.

You can see why Pochettino would be keen to talk about the red card, rather than the performance of his players. After all, United had just lost the first game of his tenure. Was the Argentine keen to create a siege mentality?
You can also understand United's frustration - two of their biggest games of the season so far have been defined by refereeing decisions.
The first was the VAR error to allow Erling Haaland's match-winning goal in the Manchester derby, when Enzo Fernandez clearly committed an offside offence.
As for the Yoro incident, Pochettino reserved much his criticism for the VAR. United felt he only took a cursory look at where the ball would run.
It should be noted that Match Officials Mic'd up, on which Webb gave his views, was filmed on Monday evening - before the result of the appeal.
Webb acknowledged the argument against a red card, which was Isak would not get the ball. But he was adamant it was not such an egregious error that it required a VAR intervention.
So are we back to arguing about when VAR should get involved?
The VAR threshold is too high, until it is too low. Rinse and repeat.
It is the Premier League clubs, and not Pro Ref nor the FA, who set where the bar sits.
Take the last stakeholders' survey, which helps to shape how the game is officiated.
It found 65% wanted to maintain the current threshold for VAR intervention, 20% to increase it, and just 15% to lower it.
But, of course, where the Yoro incident sits is still a matter of opinion.
'And the three points?' - Pochettino after Yoro red overturned
How confusing it must be for a supporter just watching on, hoping to understand.
An FA regulatory commission has said the red card decision was wrong. Case closed? Not so fast.
Pro Ref will not always agree with the decision of an appeal board, nor will they use it as a barometer for future decisions.
And the burden of proof for a VAR intervention is considered higher than for an FA commission.
Pro Ref places far more stock upon the judgements of the Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel.
The KMI Panel creates the merit table for referees, and helps shape how decisions are made in the future - especially for the VARs.
The FA is responsible purely for disciplinary measures and has no say on how games at the professional level are refereed.
Is there a better central midfielder on the planet than Jude Bellingham right now?

Not according to Jose Mourinho. The Real Madrid manager might be trying to manage the Englishman's minutes, but he did not hold back in his praise after the 23-year-old came off the bench and scored a superb volley , helping Real overturn a half-time deficit to beat PSV Eindhoven 5-1.
"He has physicality, he has technique, he has tactical understanding of the game, he has ambition, he has absolutely everything," Mourinho said.
"He's an absolutely extraordinary player and for me, without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world."
Bellingham's impressive 45-minute cameo came just nine days after an outstanding, all-action display for England in a 3-2 Nations League win in Spain.

While the former Birmingham and Borussia Dortmund player also earned plenty of plaudits for his displays at the 2026 World Cup, where he scored seven times, Mourinho believes Bellingham's unique blend of craft and graft isn't yet fully appreciated.

"He can play as a '10', as an '8', with two pivots, with one," Mourinho said after the win against PSV. "That's why I said, when the Ballon d'Or was discussed, that it was outrageous he wasn't among the top 10."
While wingers like Lamine Yamal or Michael Olise are also likely to be contenders for the 2027 award, is there anyone you would rather have in central midfield than Bellingham?
BBC Sport looks at what makes him so good, and who his closest challengers are.

Although only 23, Bellingham is already in his fourth year at Real Madrid and is on course for his most productive campaign since his debut season in 2023-24, when he scored 23 goals and provided 13 assists, including setting up Vinicius Jr in the Champions League final.

He has seven goals and four assists in 18 appearances this season. Only three central midfielders have more goal involvements across Europe's top five leagues, but Bellingham's all-round game is what sets him apart.
He leads his Real team-mates for possession won, duels won and fouls won. And while only Kylian Mbappe has had more shots on target, Bellingham offers far more than just late runs into the box.
He has played more passes into the final third than any other Real player, leads the club for ball carries and is second only to Arda Guler for chances created.
When Bellingham's coaches at Birmingham gave him the number 22 shirt, it reflected their belief that he could play any role, as a number 10, 8 or 4.
He has fulfilled that potential to become the complete midfielder.

While Bellingham made his senior debut with Birmingham, Vitinha also spent part of his formative years in the Midlands, scoring once in 22 appearances during a loan spell at Wolves - a spectacular long-range strike against Chorley in 2021.
But goalscoring isn't what the Portuguese playmaker is best known for - it is his metronomic passing.
The 26-year-old has played a pivotal role in Paris St-Germain's back-to-back Champions League triumphs, with manager Luis Enrique saying he "embodies the perfect midfielder".
He was named man of the match in the victory over Arsenal last season, having completed 141 of his 150 passes, matching the Champions League final record set by Barcelona's Xavi in 2011.
Vitinha finished third in the Ballon d'Or voting in 2025 but slipped to 14th this year, a ranking Luis Enrique disagreed with.
"It's a real pleasure to have a player with such physical abilities and that mentality," the PSG boss said last month. "He's at an incredible level."
Rice finished one place below Vitinha, and four below England team-mate Bellingham, in the 2026 Ballon d'Or rankings after helping Arsenal win their first Premier League title since 2004.

Nottingham Forest manager Oliver Glasner says standards at the club were not good enough when he arrived, and has questioned why some of his squad cannot speak English after being in the country for a number of years.
Forest are one place above the relegation zone heading into Friday's home game against Chelsea , winning just two of their first 11 games in the Premier League.
"Stability in a company is having standards," said Glasner. "Everybody who joins commits to the standards. I think, very honestly, the standards were not high enough.
"We have players who are here for four years, can't speak English. If you go to Italy, after three months, every player gives his interview in the Italian language.
"For me, if I want to manage in England, I have to speak English. If I want to manage in Italy, I have to speak Italian.
"Otherwise, Oliver Glasner, if you want to speak in your dialect, stay at home in Austria, everybody understands you, but nowhere else."

Forest, who narrowly avoided relegation last season but who did reach the Europa League semi-finals, have had a succession of managers in recent years and while Glasner refused to blame the upheaval for any problems he has inherited, he feels standards need to rise.
"We want to create a stable Nottingham Forest team that can consistently play in the top half of the Premier League," added Glasner, 52.
"We are a few steps away from this but we really believe we know which steps we have to take.
"We are still very ambitious but it looks to take a little bit longer than we all hoped. The goal is getting stability into this club and we're still working on this.
"We knew this is a transition season, let's say like this, where we still stay very ambitious but with a lot of problems to solve."

Glasner held transfer talks with Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis in London on Monday as the club prepares their plans for the January transfer window, when they hope to add up to five players to their squad.
"He [Marinakis] was asking 'what do you need, what do you want here to improve in the squad, the staff and the environment'," said Glasner.
"He wants the best for Nottingham Forest , he wants the best for everyone here.
"We need to improve in the squad, in the staff, in the environment and this is our discussion. It was a fantastic meeting and it was worth spending six hours travelling."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/formula1/art: Williams have had a difficult 2026 - uncompetitive and now in breach of spending rules
Williams broke Formula 1's cost cap during the 2025 season, governing body the FIA has found.
The team say they "unintentionally" exceeded the cap by £627,000. Last season, the spending limit was $135m (£106m).
Alpine were also found to have broken the rules, although theirs was a procedural breach without overspending.
Both teams have reached so-called 'accepted breach agreements' with the FIA.
Williams' involves a financial penalty, the amount of which has not been disclosed, and a 1.5% reduction in permitted aerodynamic research and development time for the next 12 months.
Alpine have also been given an undisclosed financial penalty.
Both teams must foot the costs of the investigations by the FIA into their rule-breaking.
A Williams statement said: "The breach relates to administrative costs we incurred making changes to our company structure.
"We believed these costs fell outside of the cap. Following discussions with the FIA, we have agreed to resolve the matter in line with their interpretation that the costs should have been in cap.

"The FIA has noted that Williams did not gain any sporting or financial advantage, and nor did we ever seek to. It has also noted that we acted co-operatively and in good faith throughout the review process.
"Integrity is central to what Williams stands for and we can now close this case and remain focused on our future."

The FIA said in a statement: "There is no accusation or evidence that (Williams) sought at any time to act in bad faith, dishonestly or in a fraudulent manner, nor that it wilfully concealed any information from the cost-cap administration.
"The financial regulations are complex, and the breaches arose from an interpretation adopted by (Williams) in good faith.
"Williams has accepted the FIA's interpretation and the resulting breaches."
It said Williams' breach was the equivalent of a 0.48% overspend, which "falls at the lower end of the less than 5% minor overspend range".
Williams' costs were incurred as the team tried to update their operations in order to become more competitive.
Williams had targeted the new 2026 regulations as an opportunity to make a significant step forwards in the team's attempt to return to the front of F1.
Instead, the team have taken a step backwards, and after finishing fifth in 2025, are lying ninth in the constructors' championship with two races remaining this season.

Alpine said in a statement: "The team accepts that it unknowingly committed a procedural breach, which is a result of inaccuracies in the full-year reporting documentation for costs related to exclusions and adjustments.

"The errors and inaccuracies in the reporting were specifically related to non-sporting and operational costs which the CCA recognised didn't give the team any performance advantage, such as marketing activities, non-F1 activities, HR activities, employees' bonus costs, offsetting of costs, and costs of inventories."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Manchester United are in the Premier League relegation zone 11 games into the season
Last season, Tottenham - a member of the so-called 'big six' - escaped relegation from the Premier League on the final day.
Now, with Manchester United making their worst start to a league season since 1972, it raises the question: are United this season's Spurs?

While Tottenham finished 17th with just 41 points last term, they actually started the season better than United have this season. After 11 games in 2025-26, Spurs were riding high in fifth with 18 points - 10 more than United have now.
But one of the biggest myths in football is 'the table never lies' and it was certainly lying about Tottenham at this stage last season.

While the table prompted talk of a possible Champions League place, expected goals (xG) had already recognised a relegation battle lay ahead for Tottenham, even predicting the position they'd finish in.
United's expected goal difference is almost identical to Tottenham's at this stage last season, but this time the table is more honest, even if United are perhaps not as bad as it makes out.
But there's no denying United's statistics are those of a team in a relegation battle, with many of them in the bottom six of Premier League teams this season.
While United have performed poorly defensively, their attack is actually not bad.
Remarkably, United have taken the most shots in the Premier League so far this season, and their expected goals scored figure is in the top five.

But what new head coach Mauricio Pochettino has to implement quickly is some quality control when it comes to shots at both ends of the pitch. United are converting just 7% of their chances and conceding 16% of their opponents' - a poor combination for any team.

And it is not simply down to finishing or shot-stopping, though they should have scored a few more. Based on xG per shot, United are currently taking the second-worst chances to score and giving up the easiest ones at the back.

As a result, Opta give United just over a one-in-four chance of being relegated at the end of the season (27.5%), making them the fifth-most likely side to go down after Crystal Palace, Sunderland, Ipswich and Coventry.
By analysing historical and team performances as well as the strength of opponents, Opta predict the percentage chance of each club finishing in each position.

While the above means it is more likely United will survive, it is worth noting the one position Opta predicts United are most likely to finish is 18th, with a 10.1% chance. That would mean the 13-time Premier League winners are relegated.

There is a 90% chance they finish anywhere else, but the next most likely are the three places just above the relegation zone, including a 9.9% chance of them finishing where Tottenham did last season.
History also suggests a relegation battle lies ahead for United given their poor start.
Of the 26 previous sides that had exactly eight points after 11 games, 13 survived and 13 were relegated. Among those that stayed up, only four finished more than six points above the danger zone.
A top-half finish looks unlikely. Since the competition became a 20-team league in 1995-96, no side has finished in the top half after taking eight points or fewer from their first 11 games.
Two teams did finish there more than 30 years ago but they had four more games to climb the table as teams played 42 games a season in those days.
Having said that, both were in the top half at the 38-game mark so United finishing there would not be entirely unprecedented.
It is a big ask, though, as the club have already taken 19 points fewer from the fixtures they have played than they did last season.

Formula One has never been short of rivalries, but the growing animosity between Max Verstappen and George Russell has become one of the sport's most compelling off-track storylines.
What began as a series of on-track skirmishes has developed into a very public war of words, with neither driver seemingly willing to back down.
Their latest flashpoint came at last weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, where they battled for the lead before exchanging further barbs away from the circuit .
With the pair set to meet again at this weekend's Qatar GP, attention will be on whether their latest confrontation carries over into the next round.
The answer lies in a series of incidents stretching back several seasons, with both drivers seemingly determined to have the last word.

At the start of 2026, Russell had every reason to believe he could challenge for the drivers' championship. Mercedes appeared to have the strongest car, and the Englishman won the season-opening race in Melbourne.
However, his young team-mate Kimi Antonelli, competing in just his second season, then took control by winning the next five races and has since secured the title .

Meanwhile, Verstappen has enjoyed a strong finish to the season, winning four of the last six races to move into second place in the standings. Russell sits fourth, having seen his championship hopes disappear.
Away from the track, there appears to be little love lost between them.

Speaking to the Pitstop podcast, New Zealand driver Liam Lawson recalled an awkward moment at a drivers' dinner in 2024. When Russell arrived late, the only available seat was next to Verstappen. According to Lawson, Russell picked up the chair and moved to the opposite end of the table.
It was an amusing anecdote, but one that offered a glimpse into just how strained relations between the pair had become.
And with their latest exchanges in Las Vegas, there is little to suggest the feud will cool down any time soon.

With the help of F1.com, here is a timeline of the Verstappen-Russell flashpoints:

April 2023 - Verstappen and Russell go wheel to wheel at the start of the Azerbaijan sprint race and touch several times. Verstappen's car showed signs of the contact and the two drivers have a verbal exchange after the race.
"I just don't understand why you need to take so much risk on lap one, it doesn't make sense," Verstappen said.

"I'm here to fight, I'm here to win. I'm not just going to wave him by because he's Max Verstappen in a Red Bull."

November 2024 - In the penultimate round of the season in Qatar, Verstappen was hit with a one place grid penalty following an incident in qualifying when he was found to have driven too slowly on a cooldown lap and impeded Russell.
Russell was on pole, but was overtaken by Verstappen at the start and the Red Bull driver went on to win with the Englishman fourth.

"I've been in that [stewards] meeting room many times in my life, in my career, with people that I've raced and I've never seen someone trying to screw someone over that hard. And that for me… I lost all respect," Verstappen later said.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2775510: Analysis: Beauden Barrett signing with the Bristol Bears is the headline grabber for his global star power, but of the three All Blacks recently linked with departures after the World Cup - Barrett and loose forwards Luke Jacobson and Wallace Sititi - it is Sititi's which will have by far the biggest impact in New Zealand.

The arrival of a such a well known individual who has played 150 tests will be hugely popular in south west England and it is significant because it will likely represent the most lucrative deal in Premiership history.
But from a New Zealand Rugby perspective? Not so much. Barrett's deal with the organisation runs out after next year's World Cup and he was not going to be offered a new one.

Indeed, there have been whispers that Barrett ignored suggestions from some of those close to him that he take up the release clause in his contract and leave a year early, thereby maximising his earning potential by pre-empting the traditional post-World Cup international exodus.

Barrett, who will be 36 by the time he joins his new club, did not have a happy time of it at the Blues this year, and was apparently told by the All Blacks at the start of the test season that he had slipped on the playmaking pecking order below Ruben Love, Damian McKenzie and Richie Mo'unga.
Beauden Barrett sprints in for his intercept try against the Wallabies in October - just his second test of the year.

But, despite not being involved in the first six tests of the year - something he admitted challenged him mentally - Barrett has since played an influential role at fullback in the wake of the injuries to Love and Mo'unga which pushed McKenzie from the No.15 jersey into first-five.

It must be said that Barrett has distinguished himself through his character and he showed in scoring tries against the Wallabies, Scotland (two), and England - several of which were from long range - that he has retained his eye for an opportunity, not to mention his pace.

"Competitive" and "committed" are some of the words teammates of former Silver Ferns captain Julie Carter are using to describe her, as news of her death reaches the far corners of the netball community.
Netball New Zealand on Monday said it was deeply saddened to share the news that Carter had died, aged 60.
"Jules", or "JC" as she was often referred by her teammates, played 50 Tests for New Zealand between 1986 and 1993.
The crafty goal attack, who could also slot in at wing attack, became the Silver Ferns' 16th captain in 1992.

Carter was known as one of the great thinkers of the game, and someone who set high standards for herself and those around her - qualities that served her well as the game entered the semi-professional era.
Julie Coney was the 14th captain of the Silver Ferns and was in the later stages of her career when Carter started making a mark.
"She was selected in 1986 and played in the series against Jamaica, but then Jules just missed out making the team to travel to Glasgow in 1987 for the World Championships," Coney said.
"She was re-selected for the World Games in 1989 and we travelled to Germany for the World Games where we won gold."
Carter also played in the 1990 Commonwealth Games demonstration match when Coney was captain.
"We were all pretty proud to pave the way to Comm Games inclusion, even though we were beaten so badly on that particular day by Australia."
For Coney, what stood out about Carter was that she was "very, very committed".
Julie Coney (right) commentating in 1995 at a Test between between the Silver Ferns and England.
"Julie was such a great person within the team. She was a down to earth, no nonsense sort of girl and very committed and very very fit and gritty, just gave everything to the game on court.
"The words that come to mind for me are competitive, driven, tough and clever. She was the sort of person that you wanted on your side.
"She was also good fun off the court. She loved a good laugh with her teammates."
At a domestic level, Coney represented Auckland and often had to mark Carter, when she played for Wellington.
"I was a goal defence and she was one of the most difficult goal attacks I've ever played against.

"We had some real tussles over the years, and she was just the type of player that really got under your skin and you had to use all your smarts and skills. You had to pull your best moves, put it that way."
The majority of Carter's Silver Ferns career was played alongside goal shooter Tracy Eyrl-Shortland. The pair seemed to have an invisible connection in the shooting end.
The 1991 Silver Ferns team that contested the World Championships in Sydney.
Both stood at just 5 ft 9 in, which would almost be unheard of in today's game, where most international shooters are over six foot.
"They were an incredible partnership, they sort of came to the forefront after Glasgow, the late 80s through the 90s, Julie and Tracy were the shooters," Coney said.
The Silver Ferns won silver at the 1991 World Championships in Sydney after a heartbreaking one goal loss to Australia.
When Carter was appointed Silver Ferns captain in 1992 she was leading a rebuild after a number of retirements.
Carter grew up in Hamilton and played for Melville High School, where the great Lyn Parker was a selector and PE teacher.
Parker would go on to coach the Silver Ferns during Carter's national career.
Carter started playing her domestic netball for Waikato, where she's remembered by former Silver Fern Tracey Fear as "versatile, tough and athletic!"

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjr4: TV chef Gordon Ramsay is to lead the new presenting line-up on BBC motoring show Top Gear, which is being revived four years after it was last on air.

The BBC asked Hammond to return to the show for the new series, he said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly: AJ Odudu said being called aggressive was "very harsh" and it was "an insane word" to use about her

More than 800 people have complained to the media regulator about an episode of ITV reality show I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! in which Mariella Frostrup accused her campmate AJ Odudu of being "aggressive".
Ofcom said 887 people had filed complaints about Sunday's episode in relation to "alleged bullying behaviour" by Frostrup towards Odudu.
An Ofcom spokesperson told BBC News: "We are assessing the complaints against our rules, but are yet to decide whether or not to investigate."

The pair were seen clearing the air on Tuesday, with broadcaster Frostrup saying she was "sorry for calling you aggressive" and Odudu telling her it is "a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women".

Relations between the pair became fractious when Odudu attempted to help Frostrup cook on Saturday's episode.
Tensions flared further as they and other campmates discussed their friction and the cooking arrangements the following morning.

After fellow celebrities Wayne Rooney and Claire Sweeney tried to smooth the strained relationship in Sunday's episode, Frostrup told Odudu she was "making a drama out of a crisis" and that she had been "thrilled there was another person" who said they could cook.
Odudu responded: "You have a funny way of showing it, that's all," before Frostrup replied: "You see, that's just aggressive and that's what keeps happening."
Odudu said she felt being called aggressive was "very harsh".
Both women later had tearful conversations with other campmates, with Odudu saying "aggressive" was "an insane word" to use about her, while Frostrup said the pressure in the camp was "too much".
They included former BBC Radio 1 DJ Clara Amfo, who said: "Calling a black woman 'aggressive' when she is being anything else but is a classic microaggression."
Singer Beverley Knight wrote: "The word 'aggressive' feeds directly into the 'angry Black woman' trope. It IS hurtful and offensive."

Speaking on spin-off show I'm A Celebrity... Unpacked on Sunday, former campmate Jordan Banjo said Frostrup had handled the situation "poorly", but urged people to "give a bit of grace to Mariella, and everyone in the camp" because "you can't judge an abnormal situation by normal standards".

It is "a really weird situation that every single person's in, and I'm not sure if people go at stuff with the clearest head", he said, explaining: "You get these weird breakdowns, and I think that's what we're seeing."
Mariella Frostrup risked further tension when she told Odudu that "you don't take an apology well"
Frostrup apologised during an amicable conversation in Tuesday's episode.

Odudu told her being called "aggressive" was "triggering because in this world, navigating it as a person who looks like me can be difficult sometimes because my experience is that my emotions and my intent are completely misconstrued".
She added: "In same way that you are allowed to express yourself, I can't express myself in the same way. We're not granted the same freedom.
"You're allowed to be emotional and passionate, and I automatically go to 'aggressive'. There's no in-between. It's like I'm 'dramatic' and 'aggressive' and that's it.
"Whereas I feel like someone like you gets to go through all the emotions of life and all of those emotions are accepted and embraced and valid."
Frostrup replied that she thought being labelled "aggressive" was "a woman thing more than anything else".

"I think women who speak their mind and are forthright, that's 'aggressive', whereas a man who speaks his mind and is forthright is a 'strong man'," she said, but added that "I totally get that there's more" when race is involved.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm89: (From left) Moyin Odeniran, Mo Mahir and Tom Whittaker all made Tuesday night's final
Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Great British Bake Off final
Moyin Odeniran said he was "in shock" after being crowned the winner of the 17th series of The Great British Bake Off.
The 22-year-old from Loughton, Essex, described it as a "very busy time" as he juggled competing in the Channel 4 baking competition with completing his university studies .
Despite his dissertation being due a month after filming wrapped, Odeniran achieved a first in his political economy degree at King's College London.
He beat fellow finalists Tom Whittaker, from West Yorkshire, and Birmingham student Mo Mahir to the title in Tuesday night's episode.
"I don't know how that happened, I don't know how I got here. I can't believe it – I am in shock," the talented baker said.
"I have made friends for life and I have just loved every single second of it, and I don't think I could have asked for anything more."
Judge Paul Hollywood described Odeniran's efforts as "pure magic" after watching his jubilant celebrations with family and friends.
"He has done an amazing job because out of all the bakers he struggled at the beginning, and he actually got better and better," Hollywood said.
Fellow judge Nigella Lawson praised Odeniran as a "worthy winner", but also said the other finalists were "sensational".
The high-stakes final saw the three contestants tasked with making a citrus celebration cake, creme brulee donuts and a "spectacular tribute to iconic British landscapes".
Reflecting on his performance in the final, Odeniran said: "I didn't want to put too much pressure on myself, but I knew I had put my best foot forward.
"I couldn't have done anything better than I did and I had a great time doing it."
He said he got "quite exhausted" while filming the series and praised his mother, sister and close friends for their support.
"Earlier on, some of the challenges were quite difficult for me and I was shocked that I kept going through," Odeniran said.
"Before you get there you think you know how to bake, and by week two you question whether you know anything about baking."
He shared his gratitude at being able to learn from Lawson and Hollywood.
"I will never forget my time there and the friendships made which will always continue," the winner added.
Prior to the final, Odeniran told BBC Essex he planned to view it at a huge "watch party" at his local church .

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqrm: The substance was released near the end of US rapper Don Toliver's gig at Co-op Live on Sunday
An "unknown substance" that prompted a mass evacuation at a rap concert may be linked to robberies and stolen jewellery at the venue, police have said.
More than 12,000 people were evacuated from Manchester's Co-op Live during a performance by US rapper Don Toliver on Sunday.
One person was taken to hospital and 88 others were treated at the scene after concertgoers reported a "horrible smell" and some people "coughing up blood".
Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said officers received nine reports of jewellery being stolen during the concert but no arrests had been made and the substance had not yet been identified.
Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said there was "no wider ongoing risk" to the public.

"We are aware similar robberies have been reported at two European concerts for the same artist and will be linking in with our European counterparts to better understand the wider picture of this suspected offending," he said.
In a statement on Tuesday evening, Co-op Live said it was conducting a "full review" into the incident.
"The safety and security of our guests, artists and staff remain our highest priority, and we take that responsibility extremely seriously."
The venue, which opened in 2024, apologised to fans for what should have been an "enjoyable evening" and said it expects no disruption to future events.
The substance was released at around 22:00 GMT, near the end of Toliver's show as part of his Nitrous – Octane world tour.
Afterwards, 88 people underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were accommodated at the neighbouring Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed.
Friends Poppy Rutter and Sophie Billing say they felt "unsafe" as they left the arena
Poppy Rutter and Sophie Billing, both 19, who had travelled from Cambridge to see the concert, said it was not immediately clear what had happened.
Sophie said: "I thought something had gone wrong with smoke coming off stage.
"We started to suffer, coughing and spluttering and feeling tight-chested. A member of staff said it was tear gas.
"Security rushed in and went straight to the pit. We only left as we were starting to feel unsafe and not 100 per cent well."
She said there was "no communication", adding: "You would think Manchester would be extra vigilant, given what's happened in the past."

Posting on Instagram on Monday, Toliver said: "I just wanna make sure everyone is safe and the next show goes on properly. My heart and prayers are with everyone that was injured last night at Co-op Live.
"The only thing I love more than creating music is performing for my fans."
He also asked that people stop bringing substances into his shows.
GMP urged anyone who feels unwell or develops symptoms following the concert to seek medical advice.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqpv: Hunter Schafer first came across Blade Runner when the 2017 sequel was released
"What does it mean to be human?" is a question that's always been at the heart of Blade Runner.
The first film in the series, released in 1982, depicted a technologically advanced yet dystopian version of Los Angeles in the then-distant future of 2019.
While the movie's flying cars haven't - quite - materialised yet in the real world, Blade Runner's themes of technological progress and the threats it poses feel just as relevant.
At least that's what the cast and crew of Blade Runner 2099, a new TV series set in the same universe, are hoping.

BBC Newsbeat spoke to stars Hunter Schafer, Lewis Gribben and Dimitri Abold, plus showrunner Silka Luisa, to ask why they think themes of artificial consciousness and existential threats still resonate.
The original Blade Runner, directed by Sir Ridley Scott, is considered a sci-fi classic that had a long-lasting influence on the genre.
It told the story of Detective Deckard, played by Harrison Ford, who hunted down synthetic humans known as replicants.
Schafer says her first exposure to the series was actually marketing for Blade Runner 2049 - the film sequel starring Ford and Ryan Gosling in 2017.
"I never thought I'd have the opportunity to make an addition to the world," she says.
"And so when that opportunity came along, I was quite thrilled."
Blade Runner 2099 is set 80 years after the original film, and portrays a Los Angeles where replicants have taken over.
Schafer plays Cora, a fugitive human forced to team up with replicant Olwen (played by Michelle Yeoh), as she tries to track down an artefact that could save humanity.
Schafer stars alongside Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh in the new TV adaptation
The series lands at a time when there are disagreements about the nature of the threat AI could pose to humans .
"I think it's particularly relevant right now, especially for the youth and young people who are inheriting a world that's asking a lot of the same questions that the show asks," says Schafer.
"I think that's timely and hopefully helpful to some degree."
But Blade Runner 2099 isn't "necessarily about just AI", says showrunner Luisa.
"It's this bigger question of what is the world going to be in 15 years and how can you plan for it?" she says.
The first Blade Runner also touched on themes of corporate greed and environmental damage, which are evident in the new series.
Luisa hopes the theme of a future that "is not going to be what you were promised" resonates with viewers today.
"The idea that you were born into a world and you thought you were expecting certain aspects of your life just to roll out," she says.
"That system is collapsing. And so what will be your place in whatever comes next?"
Blade Runner 2049 won awards and scored well with reviewers, but reports suggested it didn't hit box office targets.
This was partly blamed on marketing for the film trying to appeal more to existing fans than new ones - so what would the cast say to get younger viewers on board?
"It's just a very rich world," says Gribben, who plays Cora's younger brother Elias.
Gribben also points out that Blade Runner 2099, which employed "hundreds of artists and craftspeople" according to its makers, is a celebration of traditional film-making despite its themes.
"And I think studios will rely more on technology to make better-looking movies, but they won't have that soul."
Abold, who plays Cora's human ally Bebeto, says one of the show's key messages is about "the connections that you make".
"And the connections that you make are the foundation of humanity," he says.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cky9: The museum's Our Time space will host events among 13 large installations and flocks of sheep benches

Ten years ago the Museum of London announced it would be leaving its former home to move to the abandoned halls of Smithfield Market. Now rebranded London Museum, it is set to open its doors to the public on Saturday after a £437m project. So what's it like inside?
Leaning back on a leather sofa, museum director Sharon Ament looks across a vast brick-lined space that once bustled with market traders but is now filling with its newest visitors.
"I really love this space, it just makes me smile every time I come in - it's actually joyful," she says.
The vast room, now known as Our Time, is dotted with installations reflecting living memory.

In one corner a life-size mechanical giraffe flicks its ears in front of a lit-up NHS sign representing lockdown. Another wall has remnants of London's former greyhound tracks. Near it is the old switchboard from Buckingham Palace.
And beneath the magnificent domed ceiling roam several flocks of large plastic sheep which Ament encourages people to "pull up and take a seat" on.
"There are grins on people's faces, so I think we've pulled something rather incredible off," she says.
Sharon Ament says she wants the museum to be a shared space for everyone
The museum reflects London's more recent history such as its greyhound-racing tracks - the fireplaces of the market traders' former offices can be seen behind
A visit to the new museum starts before this point as people enter through a large covered street known as Real Time.
Here, data-filled digital displays tell of London in the moment, beside a Banksy-graffitied sentry box and the last bell to be cast at the historic Whitechapel Bell Foundry .
Next they enter the former General Market with its sheep, giraffe and signage.

This is the space where events like late-night house parties and dinner clubs will be held beside shops and eateries, including former Victorian cocoa rooms that will be open 24 hours a day at weekends.
Such hints of the building's past are everywhere. Halfway up the walls are the restored fireplaces of the traders' former offices, along with twisting metal staircases that once led up to them.
"Whenever we've found historic fabric, we've restored it or kept it, and we want to show the layers of history," explains Alec Shaw, who has led the entire project.
"We wanted a museum that worked like the market, that allowed you to come in any corner and just walk across, walk through the building on your way to work, or, hopefully, stay a bit longer."
Smithfield's General Market opened in the 1880s and was in use until the 1990s
The Our Time space seen in early 2024 when water was still splashing into the building
Shaw previously showed me around the site nearly three years ago , when scaffolding and supports were holding up the walls and there were constant splashes of water dripping on to the floor.

Restoring a Victorian relic that was abandoned in the 1990s "really tested all of us", he admits, and that was before the logistics involved in designing a new museum from the venue's seven-million object collection.
Five thousand of these are now on site and another 300,000 are due to arrive for when the former Poultry Market becomes a museum space in 2028.
"We think you could take at least eight hours to see every object downstairs, and that means you're going to keep coming back.
"The best museums are those that you go, 'Right I'll do that one today. I'll do this gallery next time,'" he says.
Our Past is based in the building's basement and tells a weaving story of London through five different chapters
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9zr: Hey Duggee is among the shows which will be part of the CBeebies hub on Netflix
The BBC and Netflix are to launch a trial hub on the streaming service next month, featuring 24 CBeebies shows.
Programmes including Hey Duggee, Numberblocks and Teletubbies can be seen on a branded CBeebies hub on Netflix from 2 December.
The trial's aim is to test new ways for the flagship pre-school channel to reach audiences. The BBC is the UK's largest commissioner of children's content.

BBC iPlayer will remain the home for all CBeebies content. Some CBeebies shows such as Shaun the Sheep are already available on Netflix, but this is the first time they will have a home hub on the subscription streamer.

CBeebies shows will also be made available to Netflix members outside the UK in a distribution deal managed by BBC Studios, with the aim of driving investment into children's content in the UK. The deal does not include China.
Netflix will also commit to funding a small number of new CBeebies commissions, the BBC said.
BBC's chief content officer Kate Phillips said the corporation is "always looking at how we can help more audiences discover" its content and brands.
"This limited trial will make a curated selection of CBeebies programmes available on Netflix, while BBC iPlayer remains the home of the full CBeebies experience," she added.
Anne Mensah, vice president of Netflix's UK content said the "unique partnership allows us to work hand in hand with the BBC to support our brilliant British kids' programme makers".
She added: "We want to build a fun and safe space parents can feel good about, with content their kids will love."
The news comes against the backdrop of big changes at the BBC.
The corporation announced plans earlier this year to cut about 1,800 roles and close some programmes and services, but it has further savings to make to reach a £500m savings target.
The BBC's finances have declined in recent years as a result of falling licence fee income and rising production costs.
The corporation also faces growing competition for audiences from streaming services, gaming, social media and YouTube.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y: The first ever Children's Booker Prize has announced the eight books in the running for the new £50,000 award.
Five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories are on the shortlist, which is aimed at children aged eight to 12.
The authors in contention include former Children's Laureate of Ireland Eoin Colfer, who is best known for his Artemis Fowl series, and teacher and children's author Catherine Bruton.
Four children have also been announced as new judges after a UK-wide competition. Twelve-year-old Ibrahim from Hampshire was one of those picked from more than 4,000 entrants.
He told me he was called back into school for a phone call with chair of judges Frank Cottrell-Boyce, who broke the news. Ibrahim said he couldn't be happier.
"First Children's Booker Prize judge! On my CV - that's going to take me a long way… I'm too overwhelmed to even be excited."

Cottrell-Boyce told the BBC "it's really, really important that this is a prize for children's books. Having judges who are children will be proof of that… If the children don't love a book, it won't win."

Ibrahim, his fellow child judges and Cottrell-Boyce will be joined on the judging panel by Ghosts and Horrible Histories actor Lolly Adefope and Sanchita Basu De Sarkar, who owns an award-winning children's book shop in north London.
Ibrahim said he loves reading "because it's just a way to unwind yourself from the outside world. If you get stuck in a book, you're not getting your face out of there until you finish it".

He's far too professional to share which books on the list he likes best, but he told me when he was reading one of them recently: "I had to tell my mum to confiscate it because I couldn't stop reading it and I was getting a headache."
Cottrell-Boyce said he isn't concerned over whether the adult judges might dominate the decision-making.
"If - like me - you've been visiting schools as a children's writer for 20 years, it's a rare thing to meet a child who is too over-awed to express an opinion. They're usually very forthright".
Ibrahim proves that point. He told me "the adults are not going to control that meeting… 100% not!"

He's looking for "something that has different perspectives, you can see it in a different way. New characters, not just the same old sloppy characters that authors make all the time. They just make these books that just have the same plot line".
The shortlisted books are by authors and illustrators from the UK, Ireland, Australia and Italy. Cottrell-Boyce described the list as "full of surprises." Here it is:
The Worst Thing That Could Possibly Happen by Guy Bass, illustrated by David Roberts. Readers on Goodreads describe it as "super creepy" and "how horror for kids should be written."

War by Eoin Colfer and Andrew Donkin, illustrated by Giovanni Rigano. It's the third book in their graphic novel series and tells the story of 14-year old Kat, living under siege in an unnamed European city.

The Night I Borrowed Time by Iqbal Hussain - the British-Pakistani author and former journalist's debut Children's book weaves a story through the eyes of Zubair, a seventh son who has inherited the power of time travel and tries to fix the lives of his family.

The Rambler's Curse by Mikey Please - the fantasy-comedy by the Aardman animator, who has also illustrated the book, has been described by The Guardian as a "laugh-out-loud, shaggy-dog spiral of purposes mistook".

The Teller of Tall Tales by Liz Hyder, illustrated by Tom de Freston, was a critic's choice in The Daily Telegraph. It's about a grandmother living in a remote cabin who weaves mysterious stories for her estranged grandchild.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3qj: King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.
Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.
The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.
Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars, with the king on Monday calling him "a true giant of the music industry".

Born in Victoria in 1943, Meldrum displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.
Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.
Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.
"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," a statement from Meldrum's family said.
Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.
He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".

King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special , saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".
On Monday, an aide to the King said he had been "deeply saddened" to hear of Meldrum's death.

"His Majesty's interview with Molly is a moment he and many others will never forget - he hopes that interview will once again raise a few smiles as Australians honour Molly's legacy as a true giant of the music industry."
Elton John - a friend and regular interviewee - paid tribute to him as "an Australian legend and an institution", while pop star Kylie Minogue said she would be turning up the music in his honour.
"As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room."
"He championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way. I'm so grateful for his unwavering love and support."

Australia's Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon: "One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music."
