https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy0: As food inflation rises, vegetables are becoming an increasingly expensive part of the household budget
India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data , external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.

With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall , external , India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
Onion prices have surged, adding to the pressure on household food budgets
A survey by polling agency LocalCircles found that six in 10 consumers say household essentials cost them over 20% more each month than a year ago, prompting calls for government intervention.
Rising prices are also forcing cutbacks: 74% are curbing discretionary spending on eating out, shopping and entertainment, while half are buying smaller quantities of essentials.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.

"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.

Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis , external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.

Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.

And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.
Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm93: Between 2013 and 2026, almost 250,000 badgers were killed in England as part of widespread culling to tackle bovine tuberculosis (TB)
Plaid Cymru ministers have ruled out a mass badger cull as part of updated plans to tackle bovine tuberculosis (TB).
It follows months of speculation over the Welsh government's intentions, after an expert group warned "a step change" was needed in efforts to eradicate the disease.
While farming leaders have long called for tougher badger controls, a petition against culling has attracted more than 28,000 signatures on the Senedd website in recent weeks.
The Welsh government said it would take "a new and pragmatic approach to TB eradication that is evidence-based and science-led".
While there will be no widespread cull, targeted measures are under consideration which could involve trapping and killing some badgers if they test positive for the disease.
But further research is needed first and no timetable has been set out.
Farming unions called for swifter action, while wildlife groups warned that killing badgers was "not off the table".
Latest figures show nearly 96% of cattle herds in Wales are now TB free.
But the problem - which can be devastating for affected farms - is concentrated, with higher incidence levels in west Wales and along the border with England.
There were 10,090 cows slaughtered following TB testing in the 12 months to June 2026.
Under the previous Labour-run Welsh government, a target was set for Wales to completely eradicate bovine TB by 2041.
But before May's Senedd election an expert group set up to advise ministers , external warned that goal would "not be met", and called for urgent action and more funding.
Cattle are slaughtered if they are found to be carriers of bovine TB
The Bovine TB Eradication Programme Board's latest recommendations were published on Tuesday, alongside the government's response.
On badgers, ministers said they were "not pursuing a mass, non-selective cull".
However further research is proposed of the role played by badgers and deer in spreading the disease via new population surveys and fieldwork.

This would then lead to developing "targeted and proportionate" interventions which could include trapping and testing badgers before vaccinating or euthanising them, "where the evidence supports this".

Localised trapping and culling was trialled in Wales on nine farms between 2017 and 2024, but the cost involved drew criticism after hundreds of thousands of pounds was spent on killing a small number of badgers.
Officials told a briefing for journalists that "selective removal" of badgers was a possibility in future, but "[we] cannot give you a timeline".
In July, the Senedd backed a Reform UK motion calling on the Welsh Government to consider targeted wildlife control, including badger culling
Changes to cattle testing were also being proposed by the government, to help spot infection earlier.
They will work with the farming industry to explore "safe ways" of moving cattle out of TB restricted herds, to help businesses continue to operate.
Farms experiencing persistent issues and under so-called enhanced management will be offered more choice in how their situation is handled.
There is talk of a new advisory service for farmers and vets - and moves to provide better, more up-to-date data on the latest disease risk.
For farming families "a TB breakdown can mean months or years of restrictions, uncertainty and difficult choices", said agriculture minister Llyr Gruffydd
Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability, Llyr Gruffydd MS, said bovine TB remained "one of the most serious animal health challenges facing Wales".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq2e: An estimated 5,258 deaths in England were associated with this summer's hot weather
More than 5,000 people suffered heat-associated deaths in England this summer, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has estimated - the highest number since records began in 2016.
The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, and the estimated 5,258 heat-linked deaths were almost twice the previous high of 2,985 in 2022.
The most deadly period of the year for heat-related deaths was between 21 and 28 June, when there were an estimated 2,401 heat-associated deaths. Temperatures peaked at 38C in that period.
Climate change is expected to increase the length, frequency and intensity of extreme heat, the UKHSA has warned.

The UKHSA said summer 2026 was "exceptional", and that it recorded the highest annual number of heat episodes, which it defines as days when the average Central England Temperature (CET) is at least 20C.
There were seven heat episodes between May and August, adding up to a total of 41 days.
The UK experienced widespread heatwaves as 2026 became the hottest summer on record, according to provisional data from the Met Office.
A heatwave in May smashed the temperature record for that month by more than 2C, with a high of 35.1C recorded at Kew Gardens.
A month later, June's heatwave set another monthly temperature record - 38.0C in Lingwood, Norfolk. The previous high was 35.6C set in 1957 and equalled during the infamous 1976 heatwave.
Both were caused by heat domes - stalled areas of high pressure that trap hot air over the region.
Another heatwave in mid-August saw temperatures climb as high as 38.2C at Hartpury College in Gloucestershire, making it the hottest day of the year.
The UK's hottest day on record was 19 July 2022, when temperatures hit 40.3C in Coningsby, Lincolnshire.
A lack of rainfall this year also saw droughts declared in all of Wales and more than two-thirds of England, while wildfires caused devastation in some parts of the country.
UKHSA said the findings "underline the need for longer-term adaptation" to a warming climate, and that adapting homes, neighbourhoods and health and care settings would be "increasingly important".

Dr Ross Thompson, principal environmental health scientist at UKHSA, said this summer's hot weather had a substantial impact on public health, "particularly during the early heat episodes in May and June".
He added that periods of extreme heat are expected to become "longer, more frequent and more intense" as the climate continues to warm.
Speaking in the Commons, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said she wanted "to offer the deepest condolences to all those who lost a loved one this summer".
"The numbers are a stark reminder of the human impact of climate change, and that is why I have asked the NHS to now prepare for summer as seriously as we do for winter," she said.
During a speech at the COP31 summit earlier this month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke about the extreme weather experienced in the UK this summer, describing it as "not normal".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c: BBC Weather's Elizabeth Rizzini looks at the weather that will impact travel over US Thanksgiving.
Stormy weather on both US coasts could disrupt travel for millions over the Thanksgiving period.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicts 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.

The US National Weather Service says a series of Pacific storm systems will bring widespread rain, mountain snow, gusty winds and high surf to the West Coast this week, with coastal flood watches widely in place.

Meanwhile, Wednesday will see a storm off the south-east coast intensify and run north along the eastern seaboard. This will develop into a powerful Nor'easter storm over Thanksgiving, bringing floods, strong winds and heavy rain.
New York's annual Thanksgiving Parade threatened by approaching storm
The West Coast will be badly affected in the run up to Thanksgiving, with a strong Pacific storm expected to move into the north-west on Tuesday night and affect the area throughout Wednesday.
The storm will bring particularly heavy rain because it will tap into an atmospheric river , a huge, invisible ribbon of water vapour.
Impacts will include strong winds, heavy rain at lower elevations and snow in the mountains from western Washington to Northern California.
The AAA predicts the vast majority of holiday travellers, 72.9 million, will travel by car.
Drivers could see significant delays along I-5 between Seattle and Sacramento as a result of the storm. Mountain travel could also be affected on the I-80 and I-90.
The heaviest rain is expected to miss Los Angeles and much of Southern California.
Moderate to major coastal flooding is forecast for the California coast

With the full Beaver moon on Tuesday , the West Coast is also expecting the highest tides of the year, coupled with the incoming storm. A coastal flood advisory is in place for the Pacific Northwest and parts of California.
The worst rain is expected to come late Wednesday into Thursday, with another storm forecast for Friday evening.
The San Francisco mayor has warned that the city is bracing for significant weather impacts in the coming days.
Daniel Lurie urged Bay Area residents to check the weather forecast before travelling and avoid unnecessary journeys.
A developing storm will impact the Northeast of the US on Thanksgiving Day
On the East Coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding to the south-east.
It will hit Florida and the Carolinas on Wednesday, before moving northwards into the mid-Atlantic and Northeast on Thanksgiving Day.
The National Weather Service is predicting wind gusts of more than 40mph (64km/h) inland along the I-95 corridor, which connects 15 states and Washington DC.
Heavy rain is expected in New York City on Thanksgiving Day, with the city's emergency management authorities warning of "fowl weather" and a chance of coastal flooding.
The forecast has also raised questions about whether large balloons will be allowed to fly during the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.
Under city regulations , external , full-size balloons are not allowed if sustained wind speeds are higher than 23mph (37km/h) or gusts surpass 35mph (56km/h).
Much of the US east coast will experience heavy rain over the holiday
A major worry for the 5.96 million travellers who will take domestic flights for Thanksgiving is whether the weather will cause flight disruption.
Flights across the US have recently returned to normal after the national air-traffic control system recovered from a technical failure that prompted a rare national ground stop .
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cky9: Some have hailed the lack of consensus as a sign of a positive shift, despite the Turkey summit failure
Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming.
The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place.

Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines".

Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase".
And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all.
Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then?

The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai.
Co-leader of the negotiations Chris Bowen blamed the failure to reach an agreement on "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory"

Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed.
This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations.

Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem.
He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances.
Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty.
"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.

The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process.

And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products.
The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms.
The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, said a deal that did not mention fossil fuels was "unconscionable"

Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya.

Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm75: The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.

After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".

This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.
The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.
Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:
Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding , external
The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life
Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world
In a 2C world extreme heat is expected to be experienced in every inhabitated area on Earth
Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.

"This COP sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.
The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible – it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).
This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.
Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.
There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial , external and are not well advanced.
This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.
On the central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts – countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.
And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.
Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.
This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.
If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.
Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed

Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqzj: The waste was dumped over garden fences in South Wigston over several months
Two fly-tippers were able to dump huge amounts of household waste over their garden fences without being detected for several months, with the pile eventually reaching 20 tonnes.
It was spotted on land owned by a business in South Wigston, Leicestershire, earlier in the year.

However, due to the location of the fly-tip, it was not immediately visible to employees of the business, which Oadby and Wigston Borough Council said "allowed the offenders to act over several months".

The two individuals responsible were each issued with a £600 fixed penalty notice following an interview under caution, the authority added, while a third person was cautioned for their role in the offence.
Before the rubbish could be cleared, the council's environmental health officers worked with the business to gather evidence to prove who had been responsible.
The authority has not specified which business was affected by the fly-tipping, or from where the rubbish was sourced.
The council said it had also recently issued another £600 fine after a resident's waste was found in a lay-by off Gartree Road in Oadby.
They had not fly-tipped the rubbish themselves, the authority added, but had paid a rogue operator in good faith to take it away.
According to the council, residents have a duty of care for their waste until it is disposed of correctly and should ensure it is given to a licensed waste operator.

Councillor Samina Haq, leader of the council, said: "There is simply no excuse for fly-tipping. It damages our environment, costs money to clear up and is unfair on the overwhelming majority of residents and businesses who dispose of their waste responsibly.
"These successful cases send a clear message that we will investigate reports, gather evidence and take action against those responsible.
"Please continue to report fly-tipping whenever you see it and, if you pay someone to remove your waste, always make sure they are properly licensed."

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/indonz-featur: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/indonz_featured/2777521%2Fnot-just-a-name-on-a-list-remembering-missing-kiwi-in-nepal-shweta-mhatre
Three months after the devastating flash floods in Nepal, a mentor and close family friend of Shweta Mhatre remembered the missing New Zealander for her warmth, generosity and love for life.
Mhatre was among five New Zealanders reportedly missing after flash floods tore through the Nepal-China border region on 26 August.

The massive flash flood, triggered by a collapse of ice and rock from a Himalayan glacier, sent a torrent of water, mud and debris through a river valley, burying villages and destroying critical infrastructure.
Mhatre was part of an Isha Foundation pilgrimage group believed to have been caught in the disaster, and her disappearance has left family and friends facing months of uncertainty.
"Shweta is not just a name on a list of people missing in Nepal," hospitality business owner Sunny Kaushal said.
"I mean, she is a much-loved person who built a life, a career and friendship in New Zealand."
Kaushal has known Mhatre for more than 15 years, having first met her when she was a student in New Zealand.
"I remember her as a young woman who was enthusiastic, ambitious and keen to make something of the opportunities New Zealand offered," he said.
Kaushal said Mhatre had made the most of those opportunities in a relatively short time.
She quickly established herself in the hospitality industry and rose to a senior management role within a few years.
"She was exceptionally capable, intelligent and a very quick learner as I still remember," he said.
More than 6000 remain missing following the devastating flash floods on the Nepal-China border on 26 August, according to latest figures from Nepalese and Chinese authorities.
Kaushal said he was shocked to learn that Mhatre was among the New Zealanders missing after the floods.
"We have been hoping and praying for positive news [for] three months," he said.
"The uncertainty is particularly painful for everyone who knows her and above all, for her family."
Kaushal said Mhatre had invited him and his family to celebrate when she bought her first home in New Zealand.
He still remembers how delighted she was about the milestone.
"It was one of those occasions when you could genuinely see how proud and excited someone was about building their future in New Zealand," he said.
"These are the little memories that stay with you: the excitement, the laughter and the smile."

Four other New Zealanders - Dejan Kuzmic, Kinnari Patel, Mihir Patel and Suhasini Reddy - were also reported missing in the disaster, leaving families across New Zealand and overseas waiting for answers.

ACC has trained an artificial intelligence model to find injured people whose weekly compensation claims could be "suspended quickly", new internal documents reveal.

The model scans medical notes, correspondence with health providers, high-tech imaging and transcripts of 'recovery check-in' conversations between clients and case managers to identify claims that may no longer be eligible for entitlements.
The model is much better and faster than staff at finding cases to review and potentially suspend.
At the same time as the model has rolled out, the number of people being sent letters suspending their entitlements has increased substantially .

ACC said the model did not make recommendations or decisions, it simply flagged cases to be reviewed by a human. It said the tool had flagged 2177 claims for human review since being rolled out in June. It did not provide a breakdown of the outcomes of those reviews.
Lawyer and ACC researcher and advocate Warren Forster believed thousands of clients may not be aware of the role AI had played in their suspension.
"I think people will be shocked to know that ACC is doing it this way."
In October last year, ACC started a trial of its 'Highly Influenceable Claims Outcomes' (HICO) tool.
According to internal ACC documents its goal is simple: "The AI model should correctly identify claims that can be suspended quickly by the clinical advisors."
ACC has been under political pressure to slow the growth of long term claims.
Its 'Long Term Claims Pool (LTCP) Project' aims to "proactively address" the issue by preventing "inappropriate" cases being added and getting people to "exit" support sooner.
The HICO tool uses Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 3.5, a large language model that is embedded in ACC's cloud data platform, Snowflake.

In the trial, the tool examined the records of a target population of clients: people with contusions, sprains or strains who have been on weekly compensation for 70-365 days, have had a high-tech image in the past six months, and hold a current medical certificate indicating future incapacity.
Complex claims, severe injuries, surgical mesh, maternal birth injuries and sensitive claims were excluded from the trial.

The AI system screened eligible claims and created an "Auto Alert" task for a case manager to review before sending it to a medical advisor to assess. Staff were required to flag the task as high priority and review the claim within 72 hours.

Staff who referred a claim to a clinical advisor were told to ask "why you think incapacity is not related to the covered injury". The pre-written question put to the advisor asked whether clinical information supported that the person's symptoms were due to the injury being covered.

ACC initially tested three versions of its model, adjusting its selection criteria and prompts after the first version proved highly aggressive - with roughly 80 percent flagged for potential suspension, but later found to be false positives when checked by humans.
The second version flagged far fewer claims, before ACC settled on a third version it described as more "balanced", which flagged about half of selected claims for potential suspension.

A significant pair of 19th century Gottfried Lindauer portraits have been gifted to the national art collection at Te Papa by Vero Insurance.
The 1884 tūpuna portraits were stolen in a 2017 ram-raid at the International Art Centre in Parnell, and in 2022 were recovered by police in the Bay of Plenty, after sustaining significant damage .
While the portraits have been described as picturing Chief Ngatai-Raure and Chieftainess Ngatai-Raure, the actual identities of these tūpuna were unknown.
Te Papa Māori co-leader and acting chief executive Dr Arapata Hakiwai said while their true identities were unknown they still had a whakapapa connection to their land and people.

"Our ancestors are always present. They're in us, we carry with us and they're our past, they're our present and they're our future. So these ancestors are significant in the lives of many, many people from families, sub-tribes to tribes so it's an honour."
Hakiwai thanked Vero for the gift to the nation and said Te Papa would try its hardest to reconnect the tūpuna to their people.
Gottfried Lindauer portrait described as picturing Chief Ngatai-Raure, the actual identity of this tūpuna is unknown.
International Art Centre director Richard Thomson said even after the 2017 ram-raid on its Parnell Road building he always knew he would see the portraits again.

"I just knew, I just knew this. In 2022, two detectives walked into my office and shut the door and I said, 'you've found them haven't you?' And they said, 'yes we have, but you're going to have to keep it quiet.'"
Studio Izzo managing director and head conservator Carolina Izzo and her team had the job of restoring the portraits. She thanked Vero and Thomson for giving them the opportunity to work on them.

"We are very proud that we actually saved even the original varnish it was scratched everywhere. And when the people say what kind of treatment, we didn't know at the start, but we managed and we are very proud.

"[Both] of them had tears, damaged by glass and so the chieftainess has about seven, eight tears caused by glass, broken and the chief has about 13, 14 tears and we've been threading them under the microscope doing thread by thread mending, it took a long time and I want to acknowledge my staff, team members for what they've done."
Gottfried Lindauer portrait described as picturing Chieftainess Ngatai-Raure, the actual identities of this tūpuna is unknown.
For security reasons nobody knew what the team was working on in the lab, she said.

They also weren't able to do any of the normal scientific research that a restoration job would entail, so Izzo was looking forward to connecting with the staff at Te Papa and finding more information about the artwork.

"They were absolutely very damaged and also being working here at Te Papa and being working as a private conservator we never had the experience of having paintings so damaged and they were damaged but also carried still the mana of the portrait so it was quite an emotional journey for us."

Executive general manager consumer for Suncorp New Zealand Jane Brewer said the process to return the portraits began when staff recognised how special they were and escalated up the corporate ladder.

Health NZ has made hundreds of workers redundant since it was formed in 2022, only to hire at least 166 of them back again.
That's according to documents obtained under the Official Information Act (OIA) by the Public Service Association (PSA).
"Health NZ has identified 166 former employees across the organisation who were made redundant and subsequently returned to work for Health NZ as employees," it said.
The data did not count staff who were made redundant and returned as contractors.

Health NZ (HNZ) said it could not provide data on contractors - generally paid a higher rate than employees - as they were "generally not engaged or paid through Health NZ's payroll systems and are instead recorded through financial systems as vendors".
It said that information would take staff away from their other work for too long to collate.
The 166 staff were from across the organisation and it was not clear what their roles were and whether they were frontline, clinical, or back-office.
Agency-wide, 1907 redundancy payments had been logged in the payroll system since 1 July 2022.
"This figure has been compiled from more than 20 payroll systems and may include both voluntary redundancies and redundancies arising from organisational change."

HNZ could not immediately provide answers on how much had been paid out in redundancies, saying the request would be treated as another OIA, along with questions from RNZ about what exact roles those 166 staff were in, and the amount of time between their dismissal and rehire.

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said the data revealed "a senseless merry-go-round where health workers lose their jobs creating serious stress to them and their colleagues only to be hired back when Health NZ realise how critical their work was".

"This is exactly why we need a public good test," she said. "Before any major restructure, agencies should have to show what it will do to services and what it will really cost. A public good test would have prevented much of this waste.
"Instead, we've had short-sighted cuts that leave the country less able to cope with an ageing population and growing health needs."
The rehiring data came as part of a request by the union for information regarding data and digital staff in particular.

According to the health agency's employee payroll systems, there were 292 staff members working in a data or digital function who were made redundant since the district health boards (DHBs) were amalgamated to form Health NZ four years ago.

"Employees may be made redundant in one district and rehired in another," it said. "Employees may be made redundant from one role and continue working in another - these employees are excluded from this total."

Robyn Shearer, HNZ's executive national director for people and culture, health and safety, said the agency had combined 20 former district health boards and other health entities when it was established in 2022, and inherited a range of legacy systems, structures and ways of working.
Since then it had undergone "significant organisational change", including the disestablishment of some roles and the creation of new ones.
"We continue to actively recruit to frontline clinical and support roles across Health New Zealand," Shearer said.
Eligibility for redundancy payments was based on the circumstances at the time an employee left Health NZ.

The founder of a Pasifika film showcase says that turning down major funding is what has kept the festival going for almost 25 years.
Pollywood Pasifika Film Fest 24 is holding its final screening tonight in West Auckland, still operating on goodwill and limited resources.
Organiser Craig Fasi said he does not seek major funding from agencies due to specific expectations about how the funders want to be represented.
"I think part of the reason why [Pollywood Pasifika Film Fest] still exists is the fact that I can do what I do without complicated situations," he told RNZ Pacific.
"If there was a funding body that would just give me the money for what I want to do, then that would be ideal."
The non-profit relies on organisations and institutions that donate their time and venues to keep the festival going, which Fasi cites as one of his proudest achievements.
This year's screenings have drawn between 50 and 100 people, and Fasi expects its final one to have a very different feel.
"It's a very intimate cinema," he said. "The directors will come through and will have a better chance of being a bit more casual. A bit more informal."
Fasi said the filmmakers he showcases deserve more backing, and he hopes to one day introduce an awards system offering grants for their future projects.
One of those filmmakers is Jason Taouma, whose latest short, Tiki X 823 , re-imagines Pacific mythology in a dystopian future Aotearoa through the eyes of an explorer in a spacesuit.
Pollywood Pasifika Film Fest 24 holds its final screening tonight in West Auckland, still operating on goodwill and limited resources.
It is the third time he has screened a film at the festival. He said the first was shot in a park in a suit he made himself, while the second was slightly better resourced.
His latest film was crowdfunded through a Boosted campaign and credits Fasi with pushing him to finish it in time for the festival.
"We'd probably still be talking about it if Craig hadn't suggested we step up our game and try and get it done in time," he said.
Taouma said Pollywood makes room for stories that might not make the cut at bigger festivals, his own included, and he would welcome the grants Fasi hopes to offer.
He said the festival is as relevant as ever in an age of online streaming, where films can easily get lost.
"Festivals like this anchor us. As an anchor for our people, it's still very relevant," he said.
The final screening will be held at the Lopdell Theatre in Titirangi at 7pm on Thursday, 25 November.

A young man who needs a wheelchair says his rented home set-up prevents his independence and means he requires home help - at a cost to ratepayers.
Flynn Mitchell spends as little time as possible at his Auckland flat, even though he's paid to have ramps installed so he can move between rooms.

He has been part of a sounding board for the Laura Fergusson Trust's bold plans to invest $100 million building 160 highly automated homes for physically disabled people, designed to allow them to live as independently as possible .
Mitchell is 23 years old and has just started a summer internship, but the hardest part of his week is coming home to a flat that doesn't meet his needs.
"Home should be a place where you can rest and chill and at the moment that's my biggest struggle," he said.
"I'm stuck with a place right now that doesn't fit my needs and I come home and instead of chilling it's another battle that I have to put up with and that shouldn't be the case for anyone."
The kitchen and bathroom are pressure points - the toilet is two ramps down from the bathroom.
The toilet in Mitchell's home is two ramps down from the bathroom.

The stove is unusable, the bench in the kitchen too high and the sink too deep for Mitchell to do his own dishes - he gets government assistance for this but would prefer to be able to do the dishes himself.
"I'm essentially doing a pretty half-arsey job on the dishes, it's an old school set up."
Mitchell has Friedreich's ataxia, a neuro-degenerative disorder that since his teenage years has affected his ability to walk.
"I was born a fully normal child, I didn't have any health complications. I actively played football, was running cross country, and took part in sailing," Mitchell said.
"When I was diagnosed, very quickly within the next coming years, I became weaker, was physically uncomfortable in my surroundings. I was off balance, I was weak, very easily hurt."

He gained a Master of Business degree in Entrepreneurship and Innovation from the University of Otago, and for three of his four years in Dunedin, lived in an accessible flat with friends who were not in wheelchairs.
Flynn Mitchell has been part of a sounding board for the Laura Fergusson Trust.

"The flat that I moved into was amazing ... it was all designed for a wheelchair person and to have flatmates as well, they weren't in a wheelchair, which I found awesome because it was me and my mates in a flat," he said.
It was a shock to many when the Laura Fergusson Trust closed its rehab and respite facility in Auckland six years ago, due to years of deficits, but the trust was on the comeback.
Its chief executive Ray Finch said it had $100m funding and the first sites earmarked to start building 160 high-tech accessible homes for physically disabled people, in Auckland.
"The heartache and the conversations with families around people losing their independence or not having their own space are the things that have driven us to this point."
Finch said there were 269 disabled people under the age of 65 living in Auckland's aged care facilities who shouldn't be there.
Another 961 disabled people over the age of 40 were living at home with elderly parents.

"If they're renting and they pass away, who's going to pay the rent for their adults to remain behind? There's either going to be a wave of 40-somethings going into aged care in the coming years as parents pass away, or people that use wheelchairs being homeless."

New Zealanders may be underestimating the potential costs involved in a domestic holiday disaster, insurer Southern Cross says.
It said New Zealanders were planning more expensive domestic holidays but were much less likely to take insurance for them, than for international travel.
Since July 2024, it had paid more than $965,000 in claims for domestic holidays, including for things like rental vehicle excess, travel disruption , and the cost of non-refundable travel expenses .

Chief customer officer Jess Strange said a trip such as a guided Milford Track walk could cost $5850 for two people, a stay at the Minaret Station Alpine Lodge in Wanaka could cost more than $15,000 for two nights and a campervan road trip through the Catlins, Haast, the East Cape or Coromadnel could cost more than $2500 for a typical week.
"New Zealanders will happily plan every detail of an overseas trip and then forget that a Great Walk, a helicopter-in lodge or a summer campervan loop can cost thousands too," she said.

"Our claims show that domestic trips go wrong in the same ways overseas ones do - cancelled plans, missed flights, bad weather, injuries. A few minutes of planning when you book can protect the holiday you've been saving for."

"Here's the one that surprises people: only 34 of our 833 domestic claims were for $5000 or more, yet they made up more than a quarter of everything we paid out. Our largest single payout was $13,890, for a trip that never even got off the ground. A holiday in your own backyard can still come with a very big bill, and it's worth knowing that before you book, not after."
She said changing a trip before people left was 28 percent of claims and 44 percent of dollars paid, at an average $1831 per claim.
People who were aged over 70 had an average claim of $2628 compared to $754 for people under 30. Almost a third of claims involved a flight.

She said people should buy cover when they booked, including sufficient cancellation cover as well as adding up what non-refundable deposits and fees they had to pay. Travelers should also check their policy wording so they knew what cover, limits and exclusions would apply.
Southern Cross Travel Insurance chief customer officer Jess Strange.
Strange said people "absolutely" did not think about getting travel insurance for a domestic trip as much as they did for international travel.
"It's becoming more and more popular but there's quite a lack of education around the need for it and people don't realise the financial impact."
She said things like cancelled concerts could be very expensive, particularly if people had to fly from regional centres and booked accommodation.

"We had a customer who'd booked for a concert and their Airbnb had double booked them and so they had to move to a new hotel, a huge amount of money, and so we had to cover that claim for them and so people just don't think about the kind of admin and logistics associated to that stuff."
Cover for two adults for a domestic trip in March would cost about $135 for Southern Cross members compared to $219 for the same people travelling to Japan.

French tourist Maëlle Favregros died from blood loss after falling while crossing slippery, rocky terrain near the Brewster Glacier in Mount Aspiring National Park in February last year, findings released on Thursday said.
The 23-year-old was not wearing tramping boots or on a managed track and had discovered the Brewster Glacier trip on AllTrails.

Coroner Alexandra Cunninghame urged trampers to plan their routes using official sources - including the Department of Conservation (DOC) and Plan My Walk - be aware of hazards, stay on official marked routes and have the necessary skills and gear for alpine trips.
There were seven search and rescues in the area last year, six in 2024, seven in 2023, as well as another death in 2020.
Mountain Safety Council chief executive Mike Daisley said the coroner's findings aimed to stop such tragedies from repeating.

"Maëlle's death occurred in terrain beyond the managed DOC track network in an alpine environment where significant natural hazards exist and where visitor judgement, preparation and decision-making are critical factors in maintaining safety," he said.
The Brewster Glacier area was reasonably quiet and not many people explored it until about six years ago when suddenly there was a spike in visits and a lot of interest, Daisley said.
Trampers should use social media for ideas but not for preparation, he said.

"Social media in itself is not the problem. Use that for inspiration, but don't consider that your plan. Do some investigating and find out about the environment that you've decided just because you've seen a picture of it, and it's great to be inspired by it, but do your research."
The Brewster Glacier is accessed via the steep Brewster Track which climbs about 1000 metres over about 2.8 kilometres.
An interagency group had been set up in April 2024 to help raise awareness of the hazards in the area after a rise in people getting into trouble.
It prompted a new Brewster Track safety video to be released last November highlighting the hazards.
The Department of Conservation carried out a review of Favregros' death and had made several changes to boost awareness of the hazards.

They included installing new signs at the carpark and at Brewster Hut warning of the risks, targeted social media advertising about safety and planning for the track, and working with AllTrails so people were aware of the hazards, risks and skills needed.

"The increasing use has been mirrored by an increase in visitor incidents requiring search and rescue involvement, mainly associated with visitors getting into difficulty when attempting to access areas off the DOC managed experience, such as Mt Armstrong and the Brewster Glacier," the review said.
Brewster Hut was traditionally used as a base for alpine adventures and the department said it had been managed with the expectation visitors had the necessary skills, experience and capability.
The area had recently attracted "much lower skilled" visitors who wanted to visit Brewster Glacier, partly due to a surge in social media and visitor numbers, the department said.
The coroner did not make any specific recommendations to the department, saying it had already boosted safety messaging which would hopefully decrease the chance of similar deaths.
Favregros and her friend Arthur Boutillier had pitched their tents near the hut after walking up Brewster Track on 21 February 2025, the coroner's findings said.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/276: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/politics/2764233%2Fnelson-council-holds-emergency-closed-door-meeting-complaint-laid-against-mayor
Nelson City Council has held an emergency behind-closed-doors meeting following a falling-out between the chief executive and mayor.

Tuesday's meeting was called at the urging of the Chief Executive Employment Committee to discuss a confidential complaint process as the committee said the matter had to be dealt with and could not be delayed.
Council staff said the complaint was a confidential matter and they could not share any details about it.
The extraordinary meeting comes after concerns were raised about Mayor Nick Smith's behaviour towards chief executive Nigel Philpott, councillors and staff.

Smith confirmed to RNZ a code of conduct complaint was made against him in July after a closed-door meeting a month earlier when elected members debated whether to remove first-term councillor Lisa Austin from office over her business interests.
Austin said a code of conduct complaint had also been made against her over the same issue.
Austin and her husband own Austin Transport Tippers Ltd that supplies trucks to two council contractors for haulage work but does not have any direct contracts with Nelson City Council.

The law prevents people from being elected or appointed as a member of a council if they have contracts or subcontracts from the council totalling more than $100,000 per year unless the auditor-general grants an exemption. The amount was previously $25,000 but was increased on 6 June.
Elected members voted to let Austin remain on council and not proceed with a by-election.
Smith told RNZ there was an argument with raised voices between himself and Philpott over the decision not to disclose how councillors voted at the June meeting.
The mayor requested members' votes were recorded but alleged Philpott said the votes should remain anonymous so those voting to remove Austin were not subject to criticism.
Smith said he was put under "enormous pressure" to agree for the vote to be kept secret and the complainants alleged he intimidated councillors by saying the vote would be made public.
Code of conduct complaints were costing ratepayers tens of thousands of dollars and were "a huge distraction for Council getting on with the job for the people of Nelson", he said.
He was disappointed details of the complaint had been leaked to media and, while he respected the confidentiality of the process, he would continue to defend himself, Smith said.
Philpott said there was a confidential process that needed to be followed and it was unfortunate the matter was in the public arena.
"To protect the integrity of this process, I have reminded all elected members and senior staff that it should be treated confidentially at this stage, without exception.
"It would be inappropriate for me to comment further at this time."
Councillors RNZ spoke to did not want to comment on the code of conduct complaint.
Deputy Mayor Pete Rainey said the process was confidential, and commenting on it was "inexcusable".

"There's a bit of an unwritten rule as far as councils are concerned, in my experience, is that when council makes a decision, once a decision is made, it should be supported by elected members, whether you agree with the decision or not."

Austin previously told RNZ she had worked with lawyer Dr Mai Chen to ensure the council and the Audit Office had correct information and confirmed she was legally allowed to stand for election and be elected as a councillor.

Smith said the issue of Austin's eligibility to be a councillor should have ended in May, when the Audit Office decided it was not in the public interest to prosecute her and he was defending the democratic process by which she was elected.
https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/jordie-ba: All Blacks star Jordie Barrett has been named a finalist for World Rugby’s Player of the Year award, one of rugby’s biggest individual honours.
Barrett is one of four players in the running, along with France’s Louis Bielle-Biarrey and South Africans Malcolm Marx and Ox Nche. Marx is the reigning champion, having won the award last year.
The finalists were announced on Tuesday, ahead of an awards ceremony expected later this month. If Barrett wins, he would be the first All Black to take out the award since Ardie Savea in 2023.

Fellow All Black Peter Lakai has also been nominated, for World Rugby’s Try of the Year award. His try came during New Zealand’s big 50-19 win over Australia at Eden Park in October, when the All Blacks kept hold of the Bledisloe Cup.
In the move, Barrett won a contest for a high ball, before passing to teammate Damian McKenzie, who broke through the Wallabies’ defence and set up Lakai to score.
It caps off a strong year for New Zealand rugby, with two Kiwi players now up for some of the sport’s most prestigious individual prizes.
Fans will have to wait to find out whether Barrett and Lakai can bring the awards home, with winners usually revealed once the busy November international rugby window wraps up.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/giant-new: Northland has its first wind farm, with power company Mercury officially opening the $287 million Kaiwaikawe Wind Farm near Dargaville on Monday.

The wind farm sits at Ōmāmari, on the region’s west coast, on farmland run by Pāmu. Mercury chief executive Stew Hamilton cut the ribbon alongside Kaipara Deputy Mayor Gordon Lambeth and Northland MP Grant McCallum.
“Today we recognise the skill and commitment of everyone who has helped bring Northland’s first wind farm to life,” Hamilton said.

The wind farm has 12 huge turbines, each standing 206 metres tall from the ground to the tip of the blade when it’s pointing straight up. That makes them the tallest turbines in New Zealand, and the second-tallest structures in the whole country, beaten only by Auckland’s Sky Tower.
Together, the turbines can make about 77 megawatts of electricity. That’s enough power for more than 31,000 homes once the wind farm is running at full strength.
Construction began in March last year, and Mercury says the project remains on schedule and on budget, with full power generation expected by 2027.
“We remain on track to complete the Kaiwaikawe development on schedule and on budget,” Hamilton said.
Wind farms like this one help New Zealand make electricity without burning fuels like coal or gas, which is better for the environment and for the climate.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/millis-to: Kia ora koutou, and welcome back to Milli’s Top Five! This week I’m counting down the strangest jobs on the planet. Forget being a doctor, a builder or a teacher (sorry, teachers!). These are jobs you won’t find on any careers poster at school. Read on, then head to the Kahoot at the end to vote for the job you think is the strangest of all.

5. The Wizard of New Zealand (Aotearoa) Coming in at number five is a job that sounds like it’s straight out of a storybook. Did you know Aotearoa once had an official wizard? Ian Brackenbury Channell, known simply as The Wizard, became famous for dressing as a wizard and giving speeches in Christchurch’s Cathedral Square. In 1990, Prime Minister Mike Moore named him the official Wizard of New Zealand, and art gallery directors even called him a living work of art. From 1998, Christchurch City Council paid him $16,000 a year to provide “acts of wizardry” and help promote the city. Over 23 years, that added up to $368,000! In 2021, the council ended his contract, saying it wanted to promote Ōtautahi Christchurch in new ways. The Wizard wasn’t happy about it, but he said he would keep doing his wizardry anyway, even without the pay.

4. Train pusher (Japan) At number four is a job where pushing people is actually allowed! In Tokyo, some trains get so packed at rush hour that the doors won’t shut. That’s where the oshiya come in. Their name comes from the Japanese word for “push”. Wearing uniforms and white gloves, they gently but firmly squeeze passengers into the carriages so the doors can close and the trains can leave on time. When pushers first started at Shinjuku Station, many of them were students working part-time. Their busiest years were from the 1960s to the 1980s. In 1975, rush-hour trains were carrying more than twice as many people as they were built for. That’s like squeezing your whole class, plus another class, into one classroom! Crowding isn’t as bad today, but station staff still help squeeze people on at some busy stations in the mornings.

3. Odour tester (around the world) In third place is a job that really gets up your nose. Have you ever wondered how companies know their deodorant works? They ask professional sniffers, sometimes called odour judges or even “sniffologists”. At a Degree deodorant “Sweat Lab” run by the company Unilever, a team of sniffers checks thousands of armpits every year. In one common test, volunteers put the deodorant on only one armpit, so the testers can compare it with the other side. The testers lean in close, take a good sniff and give each armpit a score. Before they start, they’re trained using pretend smells made from chemicals, so everyone scores smells the same way. Depending on the lab, they might also have to sniff bad breath or even dirty nappies. Testers have to stay professional, no matter how stinky things get. I think I’d need a peg for my nose!

2. Professional queuer (around the world) Coming in at number two is a job where you get paid to wait. Professional queuers, also called line-standers, stand in lines so other people don’t have to. In New York, Robert Samuel runs a business called Same Ole Line Dudes, which waits in queues for its customers, even at busy airport security lines. In Washington DC, in the United States, line-standers save seats at public hearings held by Congress, the group that makes the country’s laws. Some have arrived as early as 3am, and before one big Supreme Court hearing in 2012, line-standers waited for four days! When the event is about to start, the person who paid simply swaps in. Tadeusz Żak, a professional line-stander from Poland, says the job needs honesty and lots of patience. He once stood in a queue for 40 hours. I’d want a comfy chair and a very good book!
https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/air-nz-br: Air New Zealand is flying long-haul routes from Christchurch again, after a non-stop flight to Singapore took off on 28 October 2026. Long-haul flights are very long trips, often across oceans. Since 2020, the airline had flown very few of them from Christchurch.
More routes are on the way. Direct flights to Tokyo in Japan start on 28 November, and flights to Perth in Australia start on 30 November. A seasonal service to Bali is planned for winter 2027.

Christchurch Airport is expecting its busiest international summer yet, with 21 percent more international seats than before. That’s roughly one extra seat for every five. Even so, Auckland still handles nearly three times as many passengers.

Will smaller towns benefit? Christchurch is also a hub, or meeting point, for flights to smaller places like Queenstown, Dunedin, Nelson, Hokitika and Invercargill. Ajai Jayathilakan, an aviation lecturer at Massey University, warns that these regional communities could miss out.

Figures from NZ Airports looked at routes where another airline, Jetstar, doesn’t compete with Air NZ. On those routes, fares rose 4.2 percent and seat numbers dropped by the same amount. Billie Moore, who led NZ Airports at the time, said, “Regional New Zealand is living the reality of this every day.”
Jayathilakan says the new flights are good news for the South Island. He says ideas like better-linked flight timetables could help smaller towns share in the benefits.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/famous-ba: One of the Batmobiles from the 1992 film Batman Returns is going up for auction near Los Angeles, in the United States. It could become the most expensive Batmobile ever sold.

Julien’s Auctions expects the car to sell for between US$5 million and US$7 million, which is about NZ$9 million to NZ$12 million. The current record is US$4.6 million (about NZ$8.4 million). It was set in 2013 by the Batmobile Adam West drove in the 1960s Batman TV series.
Three special Batmobiles were built for Batman Returns, which was directed by Tim Burton. Julien’s calls this one the “Number One Hero car”, and it was used in most of the film’s driving scenes.
The glossy black car is about six metres long and has two large tail fins. It still has its original paint, a Chevrolet V-8 engine, and a remote-controlled exhaust that shoots out flames.
Julien’s called it “one of the most recognised and important cinematic vehicles in Hollywood history.”
However, the new owner won’t be cruising the streets in it. The car is not street legal, which means it can’t be driven on public roads. It must also stay parked whenever it’s shown to the public.
The car has spent years on display at the Marconi Automotive Museum in California, and the auction takes place in Gardena on Tuesday.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/black-cap: The Black Caps battled through a windy final day at the Basin Reserve in Wellington to draw the first cricket Test against India on 23 November 2026.
India had scored 720 runs for nine wickets before declaring, which means choosing to stop batting. That gave them a huge lead of 352 runs.

To save the match, New Zealand had to bat for the whole day without losing all their wickets. They started at 119 for two and played so carefully that it took 18 balls to score their first run of the morning.

Devon Conway made 65 and Rachin Ravindra made 37 before both were out. Glenn Phillips, who scored a century in the first innings, made 26. He and Daryl Mitchell put on 63 runs together, and Mitchell finished not out on 49.
New Zealand were 239 for five when the captains shook hands to end the match. India were still five wickets short of a win.
In Test cricket, if time runs out before either team can win, the match is a draw.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/world-lea: Leaders and scientists from around the world have been meeting in Antalya, Turkey, for a huge United Nations climate conference called COP31 – but talks on an important part of the deal have hit a wall.

Climate scientist Dr Bill Hare, who helps write major international climate reports, said talks about climate finance – money that richer countries give to help poorer countries deal with climate change – are “totally blocked right now.”

“One of the biggest worries at this COP is that there has not been, essentially, the big plan about it,” he said. He wants wealthy countries to triple the money they give to help vulnerable nations adapt to a warmer world, such as by protecting homes from floods and storms.

Dr Hare also pointed out that a small number of countries have been blocking funding and cooperation for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the group of scientists that reviews climate research for the whole world.

On a more positive note, Dr Hare welcomed strong wording in the draft agreement about moving away from fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas, towards cleaner energy. He said it might be tricky to keep that wording in the final agreement, but he hoped it would survive.
Talks at COP31 are expected to continue as leaders try to find common ground before the summit wraps up.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/niue-ocea: A project protecting the ocean around the small Pacific nation of Niue has won one of the world’s most prestigious environmental prizes.

The Niue Ocean Wide Trust took out the Revive Our Oceans category at the Earthshot Prize, awarded at a ceremony in Mumbai, India. Nearly 7000 projects from 169 countries entered this year, so winning is a huge achievement.
Prince William and Princess Catherine attended the ceremony, along with former New Zealand Prime Minister Dame Jacinda Ardern and Niue’s Prime Minister, Dalton Tagelagi.

The prize is worth millions of dollars. The trust works in partnership with the Niue Government, and people and groups around the world can already sponsor the protection of one square kilometre of Niue’s ocean for NZ$250 each.

The money raised so far has helped fund coastal protection projects in local villages, paid for insurance in case of climate disasters like cyclones, and even helped pay for half of Niue’s high school students to learn how to scuba dive.
In a Facebook post, the trust said the win belonged to the people of Niue.
Niue is aiming to raise $32 million in total to protect and manage its huge ocean area. Winning the Earthshot Prize has now pushed them over the halfway mark towards that goal.

The group started their tramp in bright sunshine, carrying water bottles and lunch in their packs. By afternoon, clouds had gathered over the hills, and a cold wind began to blow. Soon rain was falling steadily, so the leader called for raincoats and an earlier stop beside a stream. Even though the weather changed, the group stayed calm, ate together, and finished the walk safely before sunset.
